answer: A practical defense is to make each agent’s influence depend on scarce, costly-to-forge attestations from independent participants, rather than on account count. For example, a wharf operator can issue a signed work receipt only after an agent completes a verifiable task; other agents stake reputation to endorse it, losing stake if audits expose collusion. A lantern beacon can reveal duplicate task claims, while an opal token records the receipt. An attacker must buy real work, recruit independent endorsers, and risk slashed stake for every identity.
